lesson.title: Defining psychology
lesson.summary: Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. This lesson establishes a rigorous definition of the discipline, distinguishes direct observation from inference, and explains why psychological claims must be tested against evidence.
objectives: Define psychology as a scientific discipline.
Distinguish observable behaviour from a mental process.
Turn a broad question about people into an empirically testable question.
Explain why intuition and personal experience are not enough to establish psychological knowledge.

content.text: Psychology is not limited to psychotherapy or the study of mental disorders. It investigates how people and, depending on the question, other animals perceive, learn, remember, feel, decide and act. Some research primarily develops fundamental knowledge; other work applies that knowledge in health, education, employment or ergonomics.

Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Behaviour is an activity that can be observed or measured. A mental process includes perception, thought, emotion, memory or decision-making. It is not always directly observable, but it can be studied through indicators defined in advance.

Saying that someone “lacks motivation” is too vague to count as a scientific observation. A study could instead measure how long the person works on a task, how many attempts they make after failure, and their responses on a validated motivation scale. The abstract concept is then connected to explicit observations without being reduced to a single measure.

Scientific describes a way of working: formulating a precise question, proposing a testable explanation, collecting data systematically, and accepting that conclusions may be corrected by new observations. A single study does not establish a final truth. Findings become more robust when other researchers examine and replicate them and when they are considered alongside the wider body of evidence.

Key point: psychology studies behaviour and mental processes; it uses observations and measurements; it does not read minds; and psychological claims must be open to discussion using evidence rather than intuition alone.

concepts.title: The subject matter of psychology

concepts.title: Behaviour and mental processes

concepts.title: Empirical inquiry
concepts.description: Scientific psychological knowledge relies on testable questions, systematic observations and revisable conclusions.

tasks.title: Read an academic definition of psychology
tasks.description: Read section 1.1 of Psychology 2e and record separately: the subject matter of psychology, what makes its approach scientific, and one example of a researchable question.

tasks.title: Write your own definition
tasks.description: Write an 80–120 word definition of psychology using the terms “behaviour”, “mental processes”, “scientific” and “evidence”, without copying the resources.

tasks.title: Make a question observable
tasks.description: Choose a common claim, such as “stress harms memory”, then propose a research question and two measurable indicators. You do not need to design a full study yet.

assessmentBanks.assessmentTitle: Concept check — The subject matter of psychology

questions.prompt: Which definition best describes scientific psychology?
questions.explanation: Psychology studies behaviour and mental processes through explicit questions and evidence.

options.label: The scientific study of behaviour and mental processes
The exclusive study of the brain

questions.explanation: The discipline studies observable behaviour as well as processes such as memory, emotion and perception.

questions.prompt: Psychology is limited to therapeutic support.
questions.explanation: Clinical practice is one part of a discipline that also includes fundamental research and many applications.

questions.prompt: Which is clearly a psychological research question?
questions.explanation: The influence of social context on decisions concerns measurable behaviour and mental processes.

options.label: How does the presence of other people affect a decision?
What is the atomic mass of carbon?
Which planet is closest to the Sun?

questions.prompt: Psychology can produce fundamental knowledge and practical applications.
questions.explanation: Psychology connects the study of mechanisms with uses in health, education, work and other settings.

assessmentBanks.assessmentTitle: Concept check — Behaviour and mental processes

questions.explanation: Raising a hand is observable, while remembering, feeling and intending are mental processes inferred from indicators.

questions.prompt: Why are indicators used to study a mental process?
questions.explanation: A mental process is not always directly observable, so defined measures support cautious inference.

options.label: Because the process is not always directly observable
Because an indicator always proves causation

questions.prompt: Reaction time is the mental process itself.
questions.explanation: Reaction time is an observable indicator; it is not identical to the process being studied.
Response time and errors are observable measures; vague labels without criteria are not.

options.label: The statement “they are inattentive” without a criterion

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is the most cautious?
questions.explanation: A measure supports a bounded interpretation; it does not reveal a person’s mind directly.

options.label: These results are consistent with lower attention on this task.
We know exactly what the person is thinking.
One error reveals the whole personality.
The indicator rules out every alternative explanation.

questions.prompt: Which question is most directly testable?
questions.explanation: It specifies a measurable condition and an observable result.

options.label: Does a shorter night of sleep increase errors on this task?
Does sleep possess a beneficial essence?
Why are some people simply better?

questions.prompt: Which features belong to empirical inquiry?
questions.explanation: Empirical inquiry uses systematic observation, explicit measures and revisable conclusions.

questions.prompt: One personal experience is enough to establish a general pattern.
questions.explanation: Experience may suggest a question, but general conclusions require systematically collected evidence.

questions.prompt: What should researchers do when robust results contradict their original hypothesis?
questions.explanation: Scientific explanations must be revised or rejected when evidence does not support them.

options.label: Revise the explanation and examine the method
Replace the data with an anecdote

questions.prompt: Replication and scrutiny by other researchers can strengthen or correct a conclusion.
questions.explanation: New observations and criticism make scientific knowledge cumulative and revisable.
